item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
National Zoological Park organizes  22nd Sunday Bird Walk to Promote Citizen Science and Conservation Awareness; Records 45 Bird Species
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 10:02PM by PIB Delhi

The National Zoological Park, New Delhi, organised the 22nd edition of its ‘Sunday Bird Walk @ NZP’ on 22 November 2026, from 7:30 AM to 10:30 AM, reaffirming its commitment to biodiversity documentation, environmental awareness and citizen participation in wildlife conservation.

The nature walk witnessed the participation of 10 nature enthusiasts, students, wildlife photographers and citizens interested in birdwatching and biodiversity. Guided by resource experts and dedicated volunteers, participants explored the avian diversity of the Zoo and learnt about bird identification, behaviour, ecology and their ecological significance.

During the walk, participants documented 45 bird species and more than 400 individual birds in the designated area. The observations contributed to field-based biodiversity documentation and provided participants with an enriching hands-on experience of citizen science. Discussions during the walk highlighted the ecological importance of birds, including their role in natural pest control, maintaining ecological balance and serving as indicators of environmental quality and ecosystem health.

Addressing the participants, the Director (NZP), Dr. Sanjeet Kumar highlighted that citizen science initiatives such as Sunday Bird Walks provide an effective platform to connect people with nature, develop field-identification skills and promote a deeper understanding of ecological relationships and food webs. He emphasised that systematic documentation of biodiversity, supported by public participation, can contribute meaningfully to conservation awareness and environmental stewardship. The Director encouraged nature enthusiasts and citizens to actively participate in such initiatives and become ambassadors for wildlife conservation. The programme concluded with an interactive discussion and feedback session, during which participants shared their observations and experiences, followed by a group photograph.

The National Zoological Park regularly organises Sunday Bird Walks to encourage birdwatching, biodiversity documentation and public engagement in conservation. Each walk is limited to 20–25 participants to ensure meaningful learning and interaction. Prior registration is mandatory, with registrations open from Monday to Friday each week and participation offered on a first-come, first-served basis. The registration link is available on the official website of the National Zoological Park and through the NZP Saathi mobile application.

Punya Salila Srivastava inaugurates Sleep Study Facility and Autism Lab, flags off E-cart Ambulance at IIT Madras Smt. Srivastava visits key healthcare research and innovation centres at IIT Madras, covering brain research, cancer studies and medical technologies Indigenous healthcare and assistive technologies at IIT Madras aim to improve access to affordable healthcare and support persons with disabilities and the elderly Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 8:44PM by PIB Delhi Union Health…
item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava inaugurates Sleep Study Facility and Autism Lab, flags off E-cart Ambulance at IIT Madras
Smt. Srivastava visits key healthcare research and innovation centres at IIT Madras, covering brain research, cancer studies and medical technologies
Indigenous healthcare and assistive technologies at IIT Madras aim to improve access to affordable healthcare and support persons with disabilities and the elderly
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 8:44PM by PIB Delhi

Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava today inaugurated the Sleep Study Facility and Autism Lab at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras and flagged off an E-cart Ambulance service at the Institute Hospital. Her visit also included the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre, Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, National Cancer Tissue Biobank, Healthcare Technology Innovation Centre (HTIC) and National Centre for Assistive Health Technologies (NCAHT), covering the Institute's work in healthcare research, medical technologies and assistive solutions.

 

 

The newly established Sleep Study Facility at the Campus Health Centre will provide specialised assessment, consultation and treatment for sleep-related disorders among students, faculty, staff and researchers, with support from specialists associated with Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai. Subject to institutional ethics approval and informed consent, it will also enable research on sleep patterns and different types of sleep disorders. The faculty also intends to develop indigenous, cost-effective sensors for sleep monitoring and analysis.

The E-cart Ambulance service, introduced as part of the Institute's campus wellness initiative, will facilitate timely medical assistance and convenient transportation within the campus, particularly for elderly members of the campus community and patients requiring assistance.

 

The Autism Lab initiative draws on traditional Indian medical knowledge, clinical expertise and technology to study Integrated Varmam Therapy for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), as part of the activities leading to the establishment of the Centre for Indian Medical Knowledge (CIMK) at IIT Madras. The Institute proposes to collaborate with the Paediatric Neurology team at AIIMS Jodhpur, which has experience in administering the integrated therapy to more than 800 children, to study and scientifically evaluate the treatment protocol. The initiative also envisages developing indigenous pressure sensing gloves to provide real-time feedback to practitioners, alongside research into the possible genetic, molecular and epigenetic mechanisms underlying the therapy, subject to requisite ethical approvals.

 

At the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre, Smt. Srivastava was informed about its work in developing high-resolution, three-dimensional digital maps of the human brain at cellular resolution. On 11th October 2026, the Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi dedicated the Centre to the nation and launched its mission to create cellular-resolution maps of over 100 human brains across different stages of life, including brain-related diseases. The Prime Minister also released C-STROKE, the world's first human ischaemic stroke atlas, comprising over 1,000 annotated brain sections.

The Union Health Secretary was then briefed on the interdisciplinary work of the Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, which brings together medical sciences, engineering and technology to address unmet healthcare needs. Established in 2023, the Department focuses on developing physician-scientists and engineering physiologists, with research spanning cardiovascular medicine, neurology, oncology, medical imaging, artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical device development.

At the National Cancer Tissue Biobank, Smt. Srivastava was briefed on the work of this joint initiative of the Department of Science and Technology and IIT Madras, which collects and preserves cancer tissue samples with patients' informed consent for research into cancer biology, diagnosis and treatment. A significant outcome of the Biobank's wider research ecosystem is the Bharat Cancer Genome Atlas, launched in February 2025, which aims to develop an India-specific cancer genomic database to support early diagnosis, targeted therapies and personalised treatment strategies.

Subsequently, Smt. Srivastava was apprised of work at the Healthcare Technology Innovation Centre (HTIC) on affordable and indigenous healthcare technologies, including the Mobile Eye Surgical Unit for cataract surgeries in remote areas, 3nethra for early detection of eye diseases, the Neonatal Transport Unit, iQuant for rapid diagnostic testing and ArtSens for cardiovascular health assessment.

 

 

Her visit to the National Centre for Assistive Health Technologies (NCAHT) focused on affordable assistive technologies for persons with disabilities and the elderly, including lightweight wheelchairs, power-assisted mobility devices, swimming pool lifts and walking aids for children with cerebral palsy. Among its key innovations is YD One, an ultra-lightweight active wheelchair designed to enhance independent mobility.

Smt. Srivastava was accompanied by Prof. V. Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras and Prof. R. Sarathi, Dean (Planning), IIT Madras, during her visit to the facilities.

*****

SR

HFW/ Union Health Secretary at IIT Madras/22 November 2026/1

Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:55PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 22 November 2026

 

The timeless appeal of Indian mythology found a global platform on Day 3 of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), as Nitesh Tiwari’s much-awaited epic, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend (Part 1), premiered as the official opening film of the ‘Films from BRICS’ section.

Rooted in one of India’s most enduring epics, the film brings a story that has travelled across generations and cultures to an international cinematic platform. Its selection as the opening film sets the tone for a showcase that celebrates the power of cinema to connect people beyond geographical and linguistic boundaries.

The inaugural segment also featured the felicitation of diplomatic representatives from participating countries. Mr. Saidu Dahiru Muhammed, Ambassador, High Commission of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, was felicitated by Shri Prabhat, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Ms. Erny Wahyuni, representing the Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia, and Mr. Aleksandr Fursov, Acting Consul General, Consulate General of the Russian Federation in Mumbai, were felicitated by Shri Shambhu Lingappa Hakki, Joint Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs.

Dr. Mostafa Goharifar, Deputy Chief of Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and Dr. Omid Babelian, IPIS Representative in India, were felicitated by Shri G. Krishnakumar, Chairman, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC).

Ms. Meiliza Karunia Harahap, Treasury, Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia, was also felicitated by Shri G. Krishnakumar. Festival Director Shri Ashutosh Gowariker felicitated director Nitesh Tiwari in recognition of his film, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend (Part 1), which opened the ‘Films from BRICS’ section.

The ‘Films from BRICS’ showcase recognises the importance of cinema beyond entertainment. Films offer a window into the lives, values, traditions and aspirations of different societies. They allow countries to present their own perspectives while helping audiences understand cultures beyond their borders. In this context, the BRICS platform provides an opportunity to strengthen people-to-people connections, encourage creative collaboration and give greater visibility to cinematic voices from the Global South.

Together, these films make the ‘Films from BRICS’ section a celebration of cultural diversity and shared human experiences. By bringing stories from different parts of the world to one screen, IFFI reinforces cinema’s role in fostering mutual respect, strengthening cultural ties and building a deeper understanding among nations. The showcase reflects the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, or ‘the world is one family’, and underlines how storytelling can bring people closer, even when their languages, histories and traditions differ.

Stories Without Borders: Celebrating Cultural Diversity in the ‘Films from BRICS’ Lineup

Spanning 11-member countries and 10 partner nations, the ‘Films from BRICS’ showcase at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) brings together a diverse range of contemporary storytelling across genres, languages and lived realities. From sweeping mythological spectacle and animated historical reimaginings, such as Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Rise of a Legend (Part 1) and Brenda Lígia and Edu Felistoque’s Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World, to intimate dramas and genre-blending narratives such as Nguyen Hoang Diep’s 1982, Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s 9 Temples to Heaven, Andrei Egorov’s And the Snow was Falling, Nayla Al Khaja’s Baab, Ariff Zulkarnain’s Baga: Tomorrow Belongs to No One, Luis Ernesto Donas’s Baracoa, Anastasia Kuzina’s Bo Bo, Rashid Malikov’s Cotton and Katrine Weber’s Dreaming of Serenada, these films explore themes of family memory, social pressures, resilience and ecological belonging.

United under this year’s theme, ‘Stories Without Borders’, the lineup highlights how cinema from across BRICS orbit captures distinct cultural identities while speaking to universal human emotions.

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Education
Photography competition and Bhajan evening organised in the run-up to Kashi Tamil Sangamam 5.0
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:49PM by PIB Delhi

A photography competition was organised today in the run-up to Kashi Tamil Sangamam 5.0. Students of Banaras Hindu University (BHU) explored the historic Kamakoteeshwar Temple near Harishchandra Ghat and captured the temple’s distinctive architectural features, and intricate details, gaining a deeper understanding of its historical and cultural significance.

Associated with the Kanchi Kamakoti Peetham, Kamakoteeshwar Temple is known for its distinctive Indian architectural traditions and spiritual significance. The idols of the deities forming the Shiva Panchayatana, are installed in accordance with traditional architectural principles.

One of the students who participated in the competition, Khushi Yadav, described the temple’s architecture as fascinating. She said that learning about its history and distinctive features was an enriching experience and expressed her excitement at the opportunity to experience the cultural confluence of Kashi and Tamil Nadu and learn more about their shared traditions.

A bhajan evening was also organized at the Vishwanath Temple at the BHU campus today evening. A large number of devotees and students attended the programme. They were introduced to the objectives and significance of Kashi Tamil Sangamam, along with the shared cultural and spiritual heritage of Kashi and Tamil Nadu.

The pre-event activities aim at familiarising students with the traditions, temple architecture and spiritual heritage of Kashi while strengthening cultural ties between North and South India. The fifth edition of Kashi Tamil Sangamam will be organised from November 28 to December 12, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
Film Industry Veterans Discuss the Role of Film Schools at 57th IFFI
Experts underline the importance of institutional training, practical exposure, discipline and adaptability in shaping the next generation of filmmakers
Filmmaking demands continuous practice, experience and exposure to cinema from across the world: Artur Daborski
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:43PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 22 November 2026

 

Can cinema be taught, or must it be discovered? This question set the tone for a panel discussion titled ‘The Unteachable Frame: Can Cinema Be Taught or Must It Be Discovered?’ held alongside film screenings at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa today. The discussion explored the role of film schools in nurturing creative talent, imparting technical skills and preparing aspiring filmmakers for the demands of the industry.

The panel featured Amala Akkineni, actor and director of Annapurna College of Film and Media; Anupam Kher, actor and founder of Actor Prepares; Artur Daborski, cultural journalist, vice-rector for international cooperation at Warsaw Film School, programme director of the Summer Film Academy, programmer at the Tofifest International Film Festival and FIPRESCI member; Bhupendra Kainthola, former director of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII); and Manoj Paramahamsa, cinematographer in the Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam film industries, mentor and founder of Cinema Factory Academy. The session was moderated by Vikramjit Roy, who has held leadership positions at Sony Pictures India and the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC).

Amala Akkineni highlighted the collaborative nature of filmmaking, noting that film schools provide an environment where students learn to work together and understand the interdependence of different filmmaking disciplines. She also called upon film educators to challenge prevailing stereotypes and encourage more women to pursue professional training in filmmaking. Emphasising the importance of commitment, she urged aspiring filmmakers to develop the willingness to go the extra mile.

Sharing his personal experience, Anupam Kher underscored the importance of formal training in shaping an actor’s abilities. Recalling his years at the National School of Drama (NSD), he said, “I would not have been sitting here had I not gone to National School of Drama.”

Referring to his debut film Saaransh, in which he portrayed a 65-year-old man at the age of 28, Kher credited his NSD training with equipping him to undertake the challenging role. He identified observation, imagination and emotional memory as three essential qualities of an actor. An individual’s experiences, he explained, are stored in memory and become an important resource for portraying characters convincingly.

Describing acting as an engagement with the nine emotions or Navarasas, he said an actor must be able to recall and express them in keeping with the demands of a scene, sequence or story. Film schools help aspiring actors understand, practise and communicate these emotions effectively. Advising young actors to draw inspiration from everyday life, he said, “Every experience teaches you something. What you learn as a human being will help you in your acting.”

Kher also cautioned young actors against complacency, observing that competence can sometimes become an obstacle to brilliance. Artists, he said, must continually strive to improve their skills and craft.

Artur Daborski emphasised that filmmaking demands continuous practice, experience and exposure to cinema from across the world. He highlighted the role of film festivals in introducing young filmmakers to diverse cinematic traditions and enabling them to engage with films and professionals from different backgrounds. Understanding developments in world cinema, he observed, is essential for filmmakers seeking to create something original.

Sharing the approach followed at Warsaw Film School, Daborski said students are encouraged to make films in a supportive institutional environment that allows them to experiment and learn from their mistakes. Such opportunities are important, he noted, as mistakes on professional film sets can have significant financial and practical consequences.

He also stressed the need to prepare students for the business aspects of filmmaking, including pitching projects to producers, securing funding and understanding the professional ecosystem. Exposure to film festivals, he added, is an integral part of this preparation.

Speaking about the kind of films that European festivals look for, Daborski encouraged young filmmakers to explore subjects that trouble them or issues they find difficult to accept. He noted that festivals value films that engage meaningfully with important social and human concerns.

Bhupendra Kainthola highlighted the relationship between artistic expression and institutional training. “Art can be discovered, but craft has to be taught,” he said, emphasising the value of formal education for aspiring film professionals.

He observed that success in filmmaking requires creativity to be supported by discipline, structured learning and adherence to professional processes. Drawing on his experience at FTII, Kainthola noted that many students choose film education despite conventional career expectations within their families. Public-funded institutions such as FTII, he said, have a responsibility to provide an enabling environment in which their creative ambitions can be nurtured.

Manoj Paramahamsa emphasised that professional film sets operate under multiple practical constraints, leaving limited scope for beginners to experiment and learn through trial and error.

Film schools, therefore, provide an important foundation by teaching the fundamentals of filmmaking in a structured environment. Beyond technical skills, they equip students to manage human resources, coordinate teams and work collaboratively, all of which are critical to the successful execution of a film project, he said.

The panel also discussed the growing influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on film education and filmmaking.

Manoj Paramahamsa observed that AI is increasingly being used to simplify repetitive tasks, generate preliminary storyboards and improve production workflows. Technological advances have also transformed visual production, enabling filmmakers to modify backgrounds and create sophisticated visual environments even after filming.

While acknowledging the need to adapt to technological advancements, Anupam Kher emphasised that human emotion remains central to creative expression. Referring to AI-generated virtual avatars, he said technology may be able to create images and performances, but it cannot replicate the heart and soul that human beings bring to acting.

The discussion underscored the continuing relevance of film schools in nurturing creative talent through a combination of institutional training, practical exposure and experimentation. It also highlighted the need for aspiring filmmakers to remain adaptable, technologically aware and committed to continuous learning and reinvention.

The 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), being held in Goa from November 20 to 28, 2026, brings together filmmakers, industry professionals and cinema enthusiasts from India and across the world. Through film screenings, masterclasses and interactive discussions, the festival provides a platform for cinematic exchange, learning and collaboration.

Rahman for Banaras, a…
item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
“Thousands of Years of Lived Experiences Nourished by the Ganga”: Bharat Bala and A.R. Rahman Reunite for Banaras at IFFI 2026
An intimate father-daughter drama of music, memory and legacy, set on the banks of the Ganges, has its India Premiere in the Indian Panorama section
Beyond the Familiar: Rahman Turns to Lesser-Used Ragas Like Dev Gandharva for Banaras
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:29PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 22 November 2026

 

Filmmaker Bharat Bala reunites with music maestro A.R. Rahman for Banaras, a father-daughter drama selected for the Indian Panorama section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where it will have its India premiere. The film features Abhishek Banerjee, Shahana Goswami, Neeraj Kabi, Chhaya Kadam, Indira Tiwari and Antonythasan Jesuthasan, among others.

Set against the cultural and musical landscape of Indian classical music, Banaras explores the relationship between a father and daughter, the inheritance of musical legacy and the enduring bonds between generations. The story unfolds against what director Bharat Bala describes as “the eternal spirit of the Ganges”.

Speaking about the film’s music, A.R. Rahman said that Indian classical music, both Hindustani and Carnatic, has been a constant source of inspiration throughout his creative journey. The ragas and the emotions associated with them, he said, continue to shape his musical expression.

Elaborating on his approach to the film’s score, Rahman spoke about incorporating ragas into its compositions. Reflecting on India’s cultural diversity, Rahman said it continues to inspire his musical exploration. “I enjoy every culture,” he said, noting that every language has its distinct flavour, from the potency of Punjabi to the sweetness of Bengali. He often allows languages and their cultural essence to intermingle in his music.

Bharat Bala spoke about returning to feature filmmaking after a long gap since Maryan, noting that he had worked on several short films in the intervening years. For him, making a feature film is a continuation of the creative process, undertaken when he encounters a story that he feels needs to be told.

While Banaras has been portrayed on screen in numerous ways, Bala said the city continues to offer much to explore. He described it as a place shaped by “thousands of years of lived experiences nourished by the Ganga”.

Director of Photography Marc Koninckx said his primary focus was to “catch emotions” on the actors’ faces through the use of light, camera angles, framing and composition. His aim, he said, was to make audiences feel part of the film rather than remain external observers.

“The camera is like music,” he said, explaining how he creates visual rhythm by juxtaposing colours and visual elements. He also observed that “too much colour kills colour”, highlighting the importance of using colours selectively to direct the audience’s attention and evoke emotions. This approach was particularly important while filming live at the Kumbh.

Actor Neeraj Kabi reflected on the lasting impact of the characters he portrays, saying that they often seep into his real life and become a part of him. His character in Banaras lives with dementia. Playing the role, he said, brought his own childhood to mind, a state in which the future does not exist and the present is absent.

Actor Abhishek Banerjee spoke about the challenges and spontaneity of shooting live at the Maha Kumbh, in contrast to working on controlled studio sets. Performing amid large crowds involved considerable uncertainty, he said, making the trust between the actor and director especially important. The experience took him back to his college days of performing nukkad nataks. Describing the shoot as “street cinema”, he said it transformed him both as an actor and as a person.

Rahman expressed his delight that two films featuring his music, Banaras and Ramayan, are being screened at the 57th IFFI rflecting the festival's celebration of diverse cinematic narratives and the enduring contribution of music to India's storytelling traditions.

The session was moderated by Shri Mahesh Kumar.

item.description: Ministry of Information & Broadcasting BRICS Film Festival Roundtable Explores Opportunities in Co-production, Distribution and Technology Exchange at 57th IFFI Representatives from participating countries highlight cinema's role in strengthening cultural ties and fostering mutual understanding Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:11PM by PIB Mumbai Goa, 22 November 2026 Cinema may speak in different languages, but its emotions travel across borders. Bringing this shared language into focus, the BRICS Film Festival Roundtable at the 57th International Film…
item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
BRICS Film Festival Roundtable Explores Opportunities in Co-production, Distribution and Technology Exchange at 57th IFFI
Representatives from participating countries highlight cinema's role in strengthening cultural ties and fostering mutual understanding
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:11PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 22 November 2026

 

Cinema may speak in different languages, but its emotions travel across borders. Bringing this shared language into focus, the BRICS Film Festival Roundtable at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) explored opportunities for greater collaboration among member countries, with discussions centred on co-production, film distribution, technology exchange and cultural partnerships.

The roundtable brought together representatives from Russia, Nigeria, Indonesia and Iran, along with officials from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Ministry of External Affairs, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) and Entertainment Society of Goa (ESG).

Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Shri Prabhat, highlighted India’s commitment to strengthening cooperation among BRICS countries through shared interests and lasting partnerships. Observing that cinema brings people together and offers insights into different societies, he said the diverse genres and subjects represented through films help audiences discover new perspectives.

He also referred to India’s hosting of the BRICS WAVES Bazaar in Mumbai, where discussions covered international co-productions, artificial intelligence, animation, gaming and women’s leadership. Highlighting the growing interest in working together, he pointed to opportunities for identifying production partners across participating countries. He called for stronger co-production initiatives and greater exchange of content through digital television and OTT platforms, urging participants to build on the momentum for sustained partnerships.

Shri Shambhu L. Hakki, Joint Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs, said the gathering provided an opportunity to witness the BRICS partnership through cultural engagement. He emphasised that cinema is not merely a reflection of a nation but also a means of understanding one another. Referring to IFFI’s theme, Stories Without Borders, he noted that films from BRICS countries offer glimpses into the cultural expressions of partner nations, fostering understanding beyond institutional cooperation.

Chairman of NFDC Shri G. Krishnakumar highlighted the BRICS WAVES Bazaar held in Mumbai as an initiative that laid the foundation for bringing together filmmakers and industry stakeholders from BRICS countries. He emphasised the potential of film co-production in strengthening these connections and creating opportunities for collaborative storytelling.

Shri Dipak Bandekar, CEO of the Entertainment Society of Goa, described Goa as a meeting point for cinema and cultural exchange. He observed that while films may travel internationally, the emotions they convey are universal, making cinema a powerful medium for audiences to understand the cultures and experiences of other countries.

Representatives from participating countries also outlined possibilities for collaboration. H.E. Saidu Dahiru Muhammad, High Commissioner of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to India, spoke about the country’s vibrant film industry and welcomed the inclusion of Nigerian cinema in the festival. He identified co-production and distribution as promising areas of cooperation, alongside technology transfer and capacity building, which could create economic opportunities for younger generations.

Acting Consul General of the Consulate General of the Russian Federation in Mumbai Mr. Aleksandr Fursov highlighted cinema’s ability to transcend borders and referred to film festival exchanges between India and Russia as opportunities to deepen cultural connections.

First Secretary from the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia in India, Ms. Erny Wahyuni spoke about the longstanding cultural links between India and Indonesia, reflected in shared traditions surrounding the Ramayana and Mahabharata. She proposed a familiarisation visit for filmmakers and producers as a step towards exploring co-production opportunities, alongside greater film distribution through OTT platforms. She also identified animation and gaming as areas with potential for collaboration and expressed interest in bringing cultural representatives, producers and animation professionals into future engagements.

Dr. Mostafa Goharifar, Deputy Chief of Mission, Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in India described Goa’s cultural diversity as an appropriate setting for conversations on understanding different societies. He observed that cinema offers a distinctive insight into nations and their people, and expressed hope that the gathering would lead to wider cooperation among film industries and communities.

In his concluding remarks, Shri G. Krishnakumar reiterated cinema’s role as a platform for bringing countries and cultures together. He thanked Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and Union Minister Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw for their support, observing that collective efforts could create significant possibilities through cinema.

The roundtable concluded with a screening of a short video introducing the films from BRICS countries being showcased during the BRICS Film Festival, celebrating the diversity of their cinematic traditions.

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi participates in the 5th Kaushal Deekshant Samaroh in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh
21st-century India can progress only by honouring skills; Therefore, over the past years, our government has taken a series of steps guided by the spirit of 'Shrameva Jayate': PM
When you learn a skill, you do not merely work on machines; you make people's lives easier and strengthen the nation's capabilities: PM
Today, India is advancing towards becoming the skill capital of the world: PM
I urge every young person in the country; the entire sky lies open before you today, dream big, hone your skills, and dedicate all your energy to fulfilling your dreams: PM
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:09PM by PIB Delhi


Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi today participated in the 5th Kaushal Deekshant Samaroh in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. Addressing the gathering on the occasion, the Prime Minister expressed happiness that Lucknow was chosen to host such a major skill development event, noting that as a Member of Parliament from Uttar Pradesh, it is a matter of pride for him as well.

Observing that the graduating youth have crossed an important milestone in their lives and are now set to join the process of nation-building directly, the Prime Minister emphasized that the skills and craftsmanship they acquired at ITIs serve as a major driving force for a Viksit Bharat. He added that any nation progresses capably in this very manner through the skills of its youth. Highlighting India's long-standing respect for craftsmanship, he cited Lucknow's Chikankari, fine muslin, Banaras and Kanjeevaram silk, Kashmir Pashmina, cotton textiles, Kalamkari, steel for the world's finest swords, and bronze and Panchdhatu idols as hundreds of traditional crafts that once formed society's foundational pillars. “For a long time, India's identity in the world has been through such skills,” observed PM Modi.

Explaining that India's earlier social system was structured around skills, the Prime Minister shared the example of Gujarat's Vasavaya tradition, under which skilled artisans who sustained village life settled wherever a new village was established. “These were such skilled people without whom it was difficult even to imagine village life,” remarked Shri Modi.

Pointing out that while such a system existed across every region of India since ancient times, it gradually lost importance, the Prime Minister recalled an exercise he assigned to officers as Chief Minister of Gujarat to list every task and service a person needs from waking up to sleeping and from birth to death, which yielded around one thousand essential skills that kept society moving. “I asked the officers to focus on this very thing, and then a modern ecosystem of skill development was created there in Gujarat,” noted PM Modi.

Attributing the decline of India's skill ecosystem to the colonial education system which reduced a skill-based society to producing paper clerks while the British advanced their own industry and manufacturing, the Prime Minister observed that clerical jobs came to be revered even after independence while skilled craftspeople were subjected to an inferiority complex and began shying away from their trades. “Our country has had to suffer a huge loss due to this mentality of slavery,” asserted Shri Modi.

Highlighting the government's successive initiatives driven by the spirit of Shrameva Jayate, including extending the tradition of convocations beyond college and university degree holders to ITI skill certificate recipients and placing strong emphasis on skill development in the new National Education Policy, the Prime Minister underscored the importance of honoring craftsmanship. “The India of the 21st century can move forward only by giving respect to skill,” asserted PM Modi.

Addressing widespread discussions and anxieties about Artificial Intelligence taking away jobs in the modern era, the Prime Minister recalled how during the COVID pandemic, when everyone felt helpless, it was skilled workers who managed critical operations and kept things running. “Understand this point of mine very well: whoever has skill, no one can take away their employment,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Emphasizing that learning a craft goes beyond operating machines to making people's lives easier while strengthening national capability and manufacturing capacity, the Prime Minister highlighted the unprecedented focus on ITIs since 2014, noting that nearly 5,000 new ITIs have been built in a single decade. “The number of those studying in ITIs has also increased by more than 5 lakh, and in this too, the number of girls has become more than two and a half times,” noted PM Modi.

Highlighting the focus on training, quality, faculty, and infrastructure in ITIs, which had previously lagged behind with outdated trades, the Prime Minister noted that over 30 new-age trades have now been introduced, including Aeronautical Structure, Artificial Intelligence Assistant, Cyber Security Assistant, Drone Technician, Green Hydrogen Technician, Industrial Robotics, Electric Vehicles, Animation and Special Effects, and Semiconductor Technician, designed for both Indian and global needs alongside India's ongoing trade agreements and FTA discussions. “All of this is being done for you, the youth; new opportunities are being created for your future,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Detailing efforts to modernize ITI curricula and machinery, train instructors in new technologies, and build direct links between training and industry, the Prime Minister highlighted the investment of 60,000 crore rupees under the PM-SETU scheme.“Our youth are going to benefit immensely from this,” affirmed PM Modi.

Noting that India's rapid development is generating vast employment opportunities for skilled workers, the Prime Minister pointed to the 50 crore people lifted out of poverty over the past 12 to 13 years through government facilities that instilled confidence. Citing mega campaigns such as building 4 crore houses for the poor, laying water pipelines, and delivering first-time electricity lines where electricians, carpenters, and other skilled youth found work, he underlined the scale of job creation. “In this mega campaign, lakhs and lakhs of new opportunities were also created for skilled workers in the country,” observed Shri Modi.

Highlighting rising skill demand across emerging sectors, the Prime Minister cited the disruption in gas supplies during the West Asia conflict a few months ago, when the government targeted at least one lakh PNG connections per day and review meetings repeatedly flagged a shortage of plumbers delaying targets, while pointing to huge skilled manpower needs in solar power and the burgeoning sports economy spanning sports equipment manufacturing and fitness. “If you are skilled, you have that many more opportunities to get employment,” asserted PM Modi.

Announcing that India is advancing toward becoming the skill capital of the world, the Prime Minister shared good news for youth and Uttar Pradesh that India will host the WorldSkills Asia competition in 2027 in Greater Noida, welcoming youth from numerous countries. “I extend advance best wishes to UP for this as well,” remarked Shri Modi.

Praising Uttar Pradesh for accelerating national development, the Prime Minister credited the present government under Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath for transforming the state into an expressway state with multiple international airports, major universities, flourishing tourism, large mobile manufacturing plants, an upcoming chip factory, and manufacturing of BrahMos, which shook the enemy in Operation Sindoor. “Because of all these development works happening in UP, new opportunities are being created for you youth,” observed PM Modi.

Recalling a recent interaction during a factory inauguration in his parliamentary constituency of Banaras where a young woman told him she now returns home comfortably even at 11 PM, the Prime Minister credited the current government under Yogi Adityanath for creating an environment of security, asserting that the sense of security and confidence of prosperity will build a Viksit Bharat, and extended his heartiest best wishes to all youth. “The entire sky is before you at this time; dream big, develop your skills, and put your full strength into fulfilling your dreams,” asserted Shri Modi.

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
‘Ruby-Cube’ Explores the Complexities of Human Relationships and the Indian Family System: Director P. Sheshadri Interacts with Media at 57th IFFI
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 7:05PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 22 November 2026

 

The team of Kannada feature film Ruby-Cube interacted with the media at a press conference held on the sidelines of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Panaji, Goa, today. The interaction featured acclaimed filmmaker and Director P. Sheshadri and lead actor Vainidhi Jagadish.

Sharing his approach to filmmaking, P. Sheshadri said that he does not actively pursue stories but allows them to come to him. He explained that he makes a film only when a story genuinely appeals to him and he feels compelled to bring it to the screen. Describing Ruby-Cube as his 13th feature film, he said the narrative is rooted in real-life experiences and draws from the complexities of the Indian family system and the way relationships evolve within it.

The Director explained that the film explores several human issues and challenges through the lives of its characters. Comparing life to a Rubik’s Cube, he said that just as the puzzle has multiple colours and combinations, human lives too have different shades and dimensions. He emphasised that his films are not necessarily intended to deliver a specific message but to establish an emotional connection with audiences. He observed that IFFI provides an important platform for films to reach wider audiences, gain visibility and receive meaningful responses from cinema lovers.

Lead actor Vainidhi Jagadish spoke about the emotional layers of her character and the film's central premise, which revolves around a daughter returning to her parental home and gradually witnessing the dynamics of her parents' relationship. She highlighted how the film reflects contemporary family realities, where individuals often lead different lives while navigating changing relationships, expectations and emotional challenges. Describing about the film she said that the story is subtle and understated, focusing on everyday human experiences rather than dramatic expressions.

Set against the backdrop of a short vacation in a hill station, Ruby-Cube brings three generations of a family together under one roof. The story follows Rohini, a psychologist, who reunites with her former husband Moorthy when their daughter Chitra brings them together while dealing with challenges in her own marriage. As the family spends time together, unresolved emotions, old relationships and questions of responsibility gradually surface.

The interaction at IFFI 2026 offered audiences and the media an insight into the creative vision behind Ruby-Cube and its exploration of contemporary family relationships. The film's screening at the festival adds to IFFI's celebration of diverse cinematic voices and storytelling traditions across borders.

The press conference was moderated by Sri. Animesh Vaze.

item.title: Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah inaugurates 12th Battalion campus of NDRF in Itanagar
item.dc:creator: Ministry of Home Affairs
item.description: Ministry of Home Affairs Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah inaugurates 12th Battalion campus of NDRF in Itanagar NDRF 12th Battalion campus will serve not only Arunachal Pradesh and Northeast but also several adjoining regions in responding to natural disasters Training for SDRFs of all eight northeastern states will also be conducted at this campus Central Government will extend all possible assistance for round-the-clock disaster relief operations in Northeast NDRF will soon emerge as a leading disaster response force among all such agencies in the world Under…
item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Home Affairs
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah inaugurates 12th Battalion campus of NDRF in Itanagar
NDRF 12th Battalion campus will serve not only Arunachal Pradesh and Northeast but also several adjoining regions in responding to natural disasters
Training for SDRFs of all eight northeastern states will also be conducted at this campus
Central Government will extend all possible assistance for round-the-clock disaster relief operations in Northeast
NDRF will soon emerge as a leading disaster response force among all such agencies in the world
Under Modi Government, the country has moved towards early warning systems, prevention, mitigation, preparedness, disaster risk reduction and a Zero Casualty approach
With the help of science and technology, advance warnings of cyclones are now available up to seven days in advance, enabling the protection of lives and property
As soon as an alert is received through the early warning system, NDRF/SDRF personnel immediately reach out to assist people
In recent years, several cyclones have passed without claiming a single life, this is a direct outcome of our advance preparedness  and effective disaster management
NDRF has conducted more than 11,000 rescue and relief operations so far, saving over 1.61 lakh lives
Between 2014 and 2026, coordinated efforts of NDRF, SDRFs and state governments have helped save lives of lakhs of citizens
Modi Govt has established a robust disaster management system by ensuring coordination among NDMA, NDRF, SDRF and State machinery
NDRF has brought pride to India by conducting disaster relief operations in several countries, including Japan, Nepal, Türkiye and Sri Lanka; 2026 declared the Year of Capacity Building for  NDRF
From 2019 to 2026, Ministry of Home Affairs successfully achieved its target of planting and nurturing more than 8 crore trees
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 6:23PM by PIB Delhi

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah inaugurated the campus of 12th Battalion of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) in Itanagar, the capital of Arunachal Pradesh. On the occasion, Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Shri Pema Khandu, Union Minister Shri Kiren Rijiju, Arunachal Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Shri Chowna Mein, Union Home Secretary Shri Govind Mohan, Intelligence Bureau (IB) Director Dr. Mahesh Dikshit, NDRF Director General Shri Piyush Anand and several other dignitaries were present.

 

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that 12th Battalion of  National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is being officially inaugurated here. Arunachal Pradesh and the entire Northeast are among the regions most vulnerable to natural disasters. All the buildings in this campus have been constructed in accordance with earthquake-resistant standards. The first line of defence against natural disasters begins with the facilities of our 12th  Battalion. This campus will serve as a centre for disaster response not only for Arunachal Pradesh and the entire Northeast but also for several neighbouring regions. Training for the State Disaster Response Forces (SDRFs) of all eight Northeastern states will also be conducted here.

Shri Amit Shah said that an Olympic-size swimming pool and a diving tank have also been constructed here for the training of personnel. This Olympic-size pool will be opened free of charge to all swimming athletes from Itanagar and across Arunachal Pradesh. He said that if any swimmer from the Northeast wins a medal at the 2036 Olympics, the journey towards that achievement will begin from this very pool, as athletes from the Northeast have consistently been at the forefront of winning medals in sports. The Ministry of Home Affairs has successfully achieved its target of planting and nurturing more than 8 crore trees during the period from 2019 to 2026. Shri Amit Shah said that every Central Armed Police Force (CAPF) and the NDRF are actively engaged in the tree plantation drive. These 8 crore trees will certainly serve nature.

Union Home Minister said that the NDRF was constituted in the same year that the Disaster Management Act came into force. However, a fundamental transformation in the country's entire disaster management framework began under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. Earlier, the country's overall approach towards disasters was primarily relief-oriented and reactive. Governments would reach affected areas only after a disaster had struck and engage in reconstruction and repair work after the devastation. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the country has moved towards early warning systems, prevention, mitigation, preparedness, disaster risk reduction and a Zero Casualty approach. We no longer remain passive. As soon as an alert is received through the early warning system, NDRF and SDRF personnel immediately reach out to assist people and carry out effective rescue and relief operations at the disaster site. Even before a disaster strikes, not only citizens but also their livestock are evacuated to safer locations to ensure their safety.

Shri Amit Shah said that between 2014 and 2026, the coordinated efforts of the NDRF, SDRF and all the States have helped save the lives of lakhs of citizens. A comprehensive system has been developed in which not only the NDRF and SDRF personnel, but also everyone from Patwaris to NCC cadets, Scout children and Aapda Mitras working across villages remain prepared to assist people even before a disaster strikes. This provides crucial support in rescue and relief operations. No disaster can be prevented, nor can its impact be effectively mitigated, in the absence of institutional preparedness. Since 2014, the Government of India has established a robust and coordinated system by bringing the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), NDRF, SDRF, the Ministry of Home Affairs and the State machinery together, right down to the Patwari level. This system ensures comprehensive deliberations on policies, their formulation by the Ministry of Home Affairs and their effective implementation by the NDRF, SDRF and State machinery.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that NDMA has prepared response protocols and SOPs for dealing with various types of disasters and provided them to the States. Between 2014 and 2026, the operational reach and deployment of NDRF have also expanded significantly. Today, the NDRF is deployed at more than 70 locations across the country. In flood-prone areas, NDRF teams reach the locations even before flooding occurs. With advancements in science and technology, early warnings of cyclones, which were earlier available 24 to 48 hours in advance, can now be issued up to seven days ahead. All citizens are safely evacuated from cyclone-affected areas. Over the past four years, this effective system has helped protect lives and property during several cyclones.

Shri Amit Shah said that during several cyclones in recent years, not a single life was lost. This is a direct outcome of our advance preparedness.  NDRF has so far conducted more than 11,000 operations and saved the lives of over 1.61 lakh people. NDRF has not only carried out rescue operations in India but has also extended its services to several countries, including Japan, Nepal, Türkiye and Sri Lanka, bringing honour to NDRF and the Tricolour. Earlier, whenever a disaster struck India, disaster response agencies from across the world would come forward to assist the country. Today, whenever a disaster strikes anywhere in the world, our NDRF proudly represents India and reaches the affected areas to save lives. This is a significant achievement of the Government of India.

The Ministry of Home Affairs has paid special attention to three key areas concerning the NDRF: expansion, resources and training. Resources do not merely mean budgetary allocations; the Ministry has also played an important role in ensuring the availability of modern equipment. The year 2026 has been declared the Year of Capacity Building for the National Disaster Response Force.

Shri Amit Shah said that soon NDRF would have emerged as a leading disaster response force among all such agencies across the world. Northeast India is an extremely important part of our country. It shares borders with several countries and plays a crucial role in many important national initiatives. Today, an NDRF battalion has been established near Itanagar in the border region of Arunachal Pradesh. Our NDRF personnel will be capable of protecting the entire Northeast from disasters, demonstrating their valour and ensuring positive outcomes. The Central Government will extend all possible assistance to the entire Northeastern region, and round-the-clock operations will be conducted throughout the year to save the lives of thousands and lakhs of people in the region.

***

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Culture
First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum Concludes in New Delhi, Reaffirming Shared Heritage and Strengthening Cultural Cooperation Among Member Nations
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 6:12PM by PIB Delhi

The First Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum was organised jointly by the Ministry of Culture, and the Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) serving as the Knowledge Partner. The Forum was inaugurated by the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi, on 20 November 2026 at the historic Purana Qila, New Delhi. It brought together 116 delegates from 22 countries, including four Ministers and the Secretary General of the SCO, Mr. Nurlan Yermekbayev. Deputy Ministers, Ambassadors, senior government officials, scholars, subject experts, cultural representatives and officials of the SCO Secretariat were also part of the gathering.

Conceived as a platform for dialogue among the diverse civilisational traditions of the SCO region, the Forum enabled participating countries to reflect on their historical interconnections and consider how these enduring links could inform contemporary cultural cooperation. Across three days, the programme combined high-level deliberations, thematic exchanges, heritage engagements and cultural presentations.

20 November 2026 - Inaugural Session

The inaugural-day programme commenced with a cultural presentation, followed by the screening of a short film on the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. The programme also featured two exhibitions at Purana Qila. “ASTITVA - The Essence of Our Existence” presented the archaeological and cultural layers of Delhi, while the “Mahabharat Scroll Pavilion” displayed a rare eighteenth-century illustrated Mahabharata scroll, offering a glimpse into India’s manuscript and artistic heritage.

In his inaugural address, the Hon’ble Prime Minister emphasised that civilisational dialogue can make a meaningful contribution to peace, mutual understanding and trust among nations. He recalled India’s historical cultural connections with Central Asia, China, Southeast Asia and the wider Eurasian region, nurtured through trade, scholarship, spiritual journeys and the movement of ideas and knowledge across the geography.

Drawing attention to the journeys of knowledge across societies, the Prime Minister referred to the Panchatantra, the Ramayana and the transmission of mathematical knowledge, alongside shared influences in music, architecture, spiritual traditions and artistic expression. He invited SCO countries to build on this legacy through contemporary initiatives, including the use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, digitisation of manuscripts and collections, collaborative research, joint exhibitions, academic exchanges, cultural tourism and greater engagement with young people. His address underscored the relevance of the civilisational ideal of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam in strengthening partnerships across the region.

21 November 2026

The day opened with the thematic session “Civilisational and Cultural Expressions”, chaired by the Hon’ble Minister of Culture, Government of India. Ministers and representatives of participating countries presented perspectives on their cultural traditions, historical experiences and areas of common interest. The exchanges brought into focus the importance of safeguarding tangible and intangible heritage, strengthening institutional linkages, encouraging interaction among scholars and artists, and advancing joint research and documentation.

A dedicated session organised by the Archaeological Survey of India, titled “A Shared Cultural Canvas - Artistic and Architectural Exchanges Among SCO Nations”, examined the many historical encounters that have shaped the region’s artistic and architectural landscape. Discussions traversed prehistoric and Bronze Age linkages, Buddhist art and architecture, Silk Route exchanges, Indo-Persian influences and maritime connections, while also considering collaborative approaches to heritage conservation and digital documentation.

Delegates, accompanied by the Hon’ble Minister of Culture, visited “The Light and the Lotus: Relics of the Awakened One” at the Qila Rai Pithora Cultural Complex. The visit offered an opportunity to engage with India’s Buddhist heritage and the wider Asian networks through which Buddhist thought, art and sacred relic traditions travelled. The day’s programme concluded with a cultural presentation by the Sangeet Natak Akademi, followed by dinner.

22 November 2026

The final day’s deliberations centred on two themes: “Language, Literature, Script and Manuscript Traditions” and “Monastic Trails - Religious and Philosophical Traditions”. The first session explored approaches to preserving languages, scripts, manuscripts and literary heritage, as well as the transmission of knowledge across generations and geographical boundaries. The second examined the journeys of faith and philosophy and the historical relationships linking religious institutions, centres of learning and communities across the SCO region.

The discussions provided participating countries with an opportunity to identify shared priorities and consider practical avenues for cooperation in preservation, research, documentation, academic engagement and cultural partnerships.

As an outcome of the Forum, Indraprastha Communiqué was prepared to capture the principal themes, perspectives and areas of convergence emerging from the three days of deliberations. It reflects the discussions held during the Forum and is intended to provide a useful reference for taking forward continued dialogue and cultural cooperation among SCO countries.

Read the Indraprastha Communiqué here.

At the conclusion of the day’s deliberations, delegates will be taken to the Red Fort, a landmark of India’s historical and cultural heritage to be followed by the light-and-sound show (Jai Hind) at the Red Fort, offering delegates an immersive presentation of the monument’s history and its importance in India’s national heritage.

The Forum reaffirmed the value of sustained civilisational engagement as a means of deepening mutual understanding and building enduring relationships among the countries of the SCO. By bringing historical connections into conversation with contemporary opportunities, the gathering provided fresh impetus to cultural cooperation across the region.

Read the Indraprastha Communiqué here.

****

item.content:encoded:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
Who Says Only Boys Can Roar Like Tigers? Baghuni Tells the Story of a Young Girl Challenging Gender Barriers in Traditional Tiger Dance
The Odia film celebrates courage, cultural identity and the freedom to pursue one's dreams
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 6:10PM by PIB Mumbai

Goa, 21 November 2026

 

What if a little girl decided that some traditions were meant to be danced with, not simply followed? What if she dared to enter a world where the tiger's stripes were traditionally painted on men and asked, “Why not me?”

This is the story of Mini, an 11-year-old girl from a remote village in Odisha, who dreams of becoming a Bagha Nacha performer. A traditional tiger dance form long dominated by men, Bagha Nacha is a cultural practice that Mini wishes to embrace on her own terms. For her, the aspiration is not merely about performing a dance, but about having the freedom to dream, challenge conventions and pursue her passion.

Inspired by true events, Baghuni (Dance Like a Tiger), written and directed by National Award-winning filmmaker Jitendra Mishra, tells the story of a young girl's determination to challenge deep-rooted gender stereotypes. Set against the backdrop of Odisha's vibrant folk traditions, the film explores gender barriers, social conditioning, cultural identity and the courage to question established norms. The film held its gala premiere at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa on November 22, 2026.

Addressing the press conference, Jitendra Mishra described Baghuni as a deeply personal milestone, marking his directorial debut after nearly two decades in the film industry. Recalling his association with IFFI's Indian Panorama over the years, he expressed gratitude to IFFI, NFDC and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for their support.

Speaking about the film, Mishra said that while Bagha Nacha provides its cultural backdrop, the story ultimately celebrates gender equality, courage and the human spirit. Inspired by the seven remarkable women in his own family, he emphasised that girls, when given equal opportunities, can excel beyond expectations. Rooted in extensive research in Berhampur, Odisha, the film also features local children selected through auditions across the state and trained for several months alongside seasoned actor Sabyasachi Mishra.

Acclaimed Odia actor Sabyasachi Mishra described Baghuni as a refreshing blend of compelling storytelling and Odisha's rich cultural heritage. He highlighted the contrast between Bagha Nacha, the traditional tiger dance, and Baghuni, meaning tigress, as central to the narrative, adding depth and intrigue to the film.

Sharing his experience of portraying a traditional Bagha Nacha performer, Sabyasachi revealed that he shed 30 kilograms and underwent rigorous physical and spiritual preparation to bring authenticity to the role. He also spoke about the demanding rituals and hours of intricate body painting associated with the folk art, in which the performer is revered as an embodiment of Goddess Maa Bhagabati Budhi Thakurani. Expressing confidence in the film's global appeal, he said Baghuni has the potential to set a new benchmark for regional Odia cinema and urged the media to take its message to audiences worldwide.

Producer Partha Panda expressed gratitude to IFFI, NFDC and the Government of India for honouring Baghuni with a gala premiere and providing a platform to showcase Odisha's cultural heritage to an international audience.

Through Mini's journey, Baghuni brings a deeply rooted local tradition into a larger aqnd more global conversation about courage, identity and the freedom to challenge convention. In this spirit, the film resonates with the theme of IFFI 2026, 'Stories Without Borders', reaffirming how cinema can carry local voices to global audiences and make stories from one corner of the world meaningful to another.

The press conference was moderated by Smt. Nikhitha A. S.

item.content:encoded:
PIB Backgrounder
Harnessing Small Hydro Power
Strengthening Energy Security for Sustainable Development
Posted On: 22 NOV 2026 5:46PM by PIB Delhi

Small hydropower uses the natural flow of rivers and canals to generate clean, reliable electricity. In India, projects with capacity up to 25 MW fall within this category. They suit hilly, remote areas where terrain limits larger projects and grid reach. India has an identified potential of 21,134 MW across 7,133 sites, of which about a quarter is harnessed. These projects need little land, cause minimal displacement and offer a long operational life. With sustained policy support, small hydropower can strengthen energy access across India's underserved regions.

Introduction

Hydropower, generated from the natural flow of water, is among the world's most reliable and established renewable energy sources. Amid India's evolving energy landscape, it plays a pivotal role in ensuring grid stability, energy security, and power system resilience. Hydropower provides firm, round-the-clock electricity alongside operational flexibility. As India accelerates its transition towards a cleaner energy mix, hydropower remains an important pillar of sustainable electricity generation.

Small Hydropower (SHP), comprising projects with installed capacity up to 25 MW, offers significant opportunities for harnessing India's untapped water resources. With substantial potential across Himalayan states, the North Eastern region, and other parts of the country, small hydro projects can contribute meaningfully to India's renewable energy capacity. Recognising this potential, the Government of India has introduced various initiatives to promote small hydropower development, encourage investment, and harness untapped resources. These efforts aim to expand clean energy generation while improving electricity access in remote and geographically challenging regions.

Beyond electricity generation, small hydropower offers several developmental and economic benefits. Compared with large hydroelectric projects, these installations generally require smaller land areas and can have relatively limited environmental footprints. They can promote local investment, generate employment, strengthen regional infrastructure, and support economic activities in remote areas. By complementing other renewable energy sources and diversifying the country's energy portfolio, small hydropower can contribute to India's energy security and sustainable development objectives.

Did You Know?

In India, the primary distinction between large and small hydropower projects lies in their installed capacity and the respective ministerial jurisdiction. Small Hydropower Projects (SHP) are defined as those with an installed capacity of up to 25 MW and are administered by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). In contrast, large hydropower projects, with capacity exceeding 25 MW, fall under the purview of the Ministry of Power.

 

Government Initiatives for Small Hydropower Development

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) is the nodal ministry responsible for promoting small hydro projects. The Government of India has recently approved the Small Hydro Power (SHP) Development Scheme for FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31, with an outlay of Rs. 2,584.60 crore. The scheme aims to add approximately 1,500 MW of small hydro capacity. It prioritises hilly, North-Eastern and border regions through financial assistance, project preparation support and technical capacity building.

The scheme outlines a set of targeted measures to support implementation, improve project viability, and ensure a steady pipeline of SHP projects across regions. It focuses on addressing key constraints related to financing, project readiness, and execution, particularly in challenging geographies. Together, these measures are intended to enable faster and more efficient deployment of SHP capacity.

Financial Support Structure:

  • Financial assistance to North Eastern States & International Border Districts of Rs 3.6 crore per MW or 30% of project cost (whichever is lower), subject to a ceiling of Rs 30 crore per project.
  • Financial assistance to other locations of @ Rs 2.4/1.78/2.054 crore per MW (depending on the size and location of the project) or 20% of project cost (whichever is lower), with a cap of Rs 20 crore per project.

 

Investment and Economic Impact:

  • The scheme is expected to attract investments of around Rs 15,000 crore in the small hydro sector.
  • It will also promote the use of indigenous plant and machinery, contributing to the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat while boosting local manufacturing and supply chains.

 

Pipeline Development and DPR Support:

  • To ensure long-term sector growth, the scheme provides support for the preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for a minimum of 200 projects. An allocation of Rs 30 crore has been made separately to assist central and state agencies in developing a strong future project pipeline.

 

Employment Generation:

  • The scheme is expected to generate approximately 51 lakh person-days of employment during the construction phase. In addition, it will create sustained employment opportunities in the operation and maintenance of projects, particularly in rural and remote regions.

The approval of the SHP Development Scheme marks a significant step towards unlocking India’s untapped small hydro potential. By combining targeted financial support, infrastructure development, and sustainability, the scheme is set to strengthen clean energy capacity while driving inclusive growth in underserved regions.  

Significance of Small Hydro Power for Sustainable Energy Development 

Small hydro power plays a vital role in advancing clean, reliable, and decentralised energy in India. Particularly suited for remote and hilly regions, these projects utilise locally available water resources to generate electricity close to consumption centres. This not only improves energy access but also reduces dependence on long transmission networks and enhances overall efficiency.

  • Decentralised and Efficient Power Supply: Located near demand centres, these projects minimise transmission losses, improve voltage stability, and ensure reliable power in geographically challenging areas, including border and hilly regions.
  • Clean and Cost-Effective Energy Source: Small hydro power generates electricity without fuel consumption or emissions, making it a sustainable and economically viable long-term solution.
  • Driver of Rural Development: By improving electricity access in underserved areas, these projects support infrastructure development and act as a catalyst for local economic growth.
  • Employment and Livelihood Generation: They create both direct and indirect employment opportunities during construction and operation, while also promoting small-scale industries and self-employment.
  • Environmentally Sustainable: With minimal land requirement and negligible displacement, small hydro power projects have a low ecological footprint and limited social impact. Their long operational life further strengthens their sustainability.

SHP offers a balanced solution that combines energy security with sustainable development. By delivering reliable, round-the-clock power and strengthening grid resilience, especially in remote areas, they contribute significantly to inclusive growth. Their ability to integrate environmental sustainability with socio-economic benefits makes them a key component of India’s clean energy transition.

Small Hydro Power Potential and Prospects in India

SHP is emerging as a vital and reliable component of India’s clean energy transition. It is particularly well-suited for hilly, remote, and difficult terrains where decentralised generation can deliver sustainable power, enhance energy access, and support local livelihoods. India possesses a significant SHP potential of 21,134 MW across 7,133 identified sites. As of 30 September 2026, approximately 5,182 MW (around 25%) has already been harnessed, demonstrating steady progress. The remaining 15,952 MW represents a substantial opportunity for accelerated development through focused policy support and public-private collaboration.

 

The regional distribution of this potential further reflects India’s rich geographical diversity and offers unique strengths across the country. The Northern region has 8,030 MW of SHP potential, particularly across mountainous terrains. The North-Eastern region holds 2,995 MW, positioning it as a key frontier for expansion, especially in hilly regions and the North Eastern States. The list is followed by Southern region with 5,490 MW of SHP, supported by well-developed river systems and infrastructure. The Western region has a potential of 2,912 MW of SHP, while the Eastern region accounts for 1,707 MW with strong potential in rural and tribal areas.

This distributed potential allows for a balanced, region-specific strategy. While the Northern and North-Eastern regions offer large untapped resources, the Southern and Western regions are better positioned for quicker implementation due to stronger infrastructure. With the recently approved Small Hydro Power Development Scheme, the Government of India is committed to harnessing this diverse potential through targeted incentives, simplified procedures, and enhanced financial support.

By adopting a focused yet inclusive approach, India is poised to unlock the full benefits of small hydropower, strengthening energy security, promoting inclusive growth, and advancing the nation’s goal of a sustainable and self-reliant energy future.

Northern region

The Northern region forms the backbone of India’s SHP landscape, driven by its mountainous terrain, perennial rivers, and favourable hydrology, making it particularly significant for development in hilly regions. States such as Himachal Pradesh (3,460 MW), Uttarakhand (1,664 MW), and Jammu & Kashmir (1,312 MW) dominate the region’s potential, with Ladakh (396 MW) adding strategic importance. Despite this strong resource base, utilisation levels remain moderate, indicating substantial untapped capacity.

Did You Know?

Run-of-the-river projects generate electricity by using the natural flow of river water without building large dams. A portion of water is diverted through channels and pipes to run turbines and is then released back into the stream, ensuring minimal ecological disruption.

 

 

North-East region

The North-Eastern region represents a high-potential growth frontier, particularly critical for expanding renewable energy in hilly regions and the North Eastern States.

Arunachal Pradesh (2,065 MW) constitutes the largest share of the regional potential, followed by Meghalaya (230 MW), Assam (202 MW), Nagaland (182 MW), Mizoram (169 MW), Manipur (100 MW), and Tripura (47 MW).

SHP development in this region offers strong opportunities for decentralised and off-grid energy solutions, particularly in remote and tribal areas. It can significantly enhance energy access, promote local employment, and reduce reliance on conventional fuels. With targeted policy interventions, improved connectivity, and community-driven models, the North-Eastern region can emerge as a major engine of growth for India’s SHP sector

Southern region

The Southern region is a key contributor to SHP development, supported by strong infrastructure, established energy systems, and favourable river basins. Karnataka leads with 3,726 MW, accounting for nearly 68% of the regional potential, followed by Keralam    647 MW and Tamil Nadu 604 MW. The region has achieved relatively higher utilisation levels compared to others, reflecting efficient project execution and strong grid connectivity.

With its robust infrastructure base, the Southern region is well-positioned to scale further through optimisation of existing assets and integration with other clean energy sources. It will continue to play a stabilising role in India’s SHP expansion, complementing growth in hilly regions and the North Eastern States.

Eastern region

The Eastern region offers moderate but strategically important SHP potential, particularly for decentralised development in rural and tribal areas.

Bihar (527 MW), West Bengal (392 MW) and Odisha (286 MW) lead the region, followed by Sikkim (267 MW) and Jharkhand (228 MW). The region’s river systems and terrain provide favourable conditions for small-scale hydro projects.

Expanding SHP in this region can improve local energy access, agricultural productivity, and rural livelihoods, while supporting inclusive development. With targeted interventions, improved financing mechanisms, and decentralised deployment models, the Eastern region can complement national growth.

Western region

The Western region presents unique opportunities for SHP development, particularly through its extensive irrigation and canal-based infrastructure.

Chhattisgarh leads the region with 1,098.20 MW of potential, followed by Madhya Pradesh (820 MW) and Maharashtra (786 MW). Against a regional potential of 2,912 MW, installed capacity stands at 730 MW. Maharashtra and Gujarat record relatively higher utilisation, while others continue to offer scope for expansion.

The region’s focus on canal-based and dam-toe projects provides a cost-effective pathway for scaling SHP capacity. By leveraging existing infrastructure and promoting innovative deployment models, the Western region can strengthen decentralised renewable energy generation. Alongside advancements in hilly regions and the North Eastern States, it can play a critical role in ensuring a balanced and diversified SHP growth trajectory.

Did You Know?

SHP projects on canal falls or dam toe utilise the drop in water levels in irrigation canals or just below dams and barrages to generate electricity. Water is diverted to the powerhouse and returned to the main canal after power generation, making use of existing water infrastructure.

Conclusion

The Small Hydro Power Development Scheme (2026-31) marks a decisive policy intervention by the Government of India to harness the unique strengths of small hydropower in the country’s clean energy journey. With an outlay of Rs 2,584.60 crore aimed at adding 1,500 MW of new capacity, the scheme prioritises reliable, decentralised power generation, especially in challenging terrains where other renewable sources face limitations.

Beyond capacity creation, the initiative is designed to deliver broader developmental outcomes. By combining targeted financial support, streamlined project preparation, and promotion of indigenous manufacturing, it will stimulate private investment, strengthen domestic supply chains, and generate meaningful employment opportunities in remote and rural regions. This integrated approach positions small hydropower as an effective tool for inclusive growth and regional equity.

As India advances towards greater energy self-reliance and a sustainable future, small hydro power offers a balanced solution that combines environmental responsibility with socio-economic progress. With this focused push, the Government of India is confident that the scheme will illuminate underserved areas, enhance grid resilience, and contribute meaningfully to building a cleaner, stronger, and more self-sufficient India.
